title: Migrants and a maze of deletions
shows: Manish Tewari, a Lok Sabha MP of the Congress and a former Minister of Information and Broadcasting, argues that the map of names left off the drafts follows the map of India's internal migration. He takes his figures on migration from the National Sample Survey Office's Multiple Indicator Survey of 2020-21. By his account about 26.8 per cent of people in rural areas and 34.6 per cent in urban areas lived somewhere other than their usual place of residence, and 87.2 per cent of those who moved stayed within their state. Of those who moved, 93.4 per cent of women in rural areas and 71.5 per cent in urban areas moved after marriage, and 38.7 per cent of men in rural areas and 56.1 per cent in urban areas moved for work. He says Delhi draws 64.7 per cent of its urban migrants and 64 per cent of its rural ones from other states, and that there are about 23 migrant workers for every 100 urban men in Telangana, 18 in Maharashtra, 17 in Delhi, 5 in Bihar and fewer than 8 in Uttar Pradesh. Across 18 sets of rolls he finds that the share of names left off the draft correlates at 0.50 with the survey's measure of urban work migration and at 0.56 with net migration from the Census, and he finds almost no relationship with the overall migration rate that includes moves for marriage. Where the reasons are split he puts deaths at 1.5 to 4.2 per cent of each state's roll, and electors marked shifted or absent at 4.3 per cent in West Bengal and 29.9 per cent in Delhi. He names Uttar Pradesh, a large sender of labour that marked 14.06 per cent of its electors shifted or absent, and Odisha, which he says has a high count of urban work migrants and the lowest share left off, as exceptions. He argues that the revision has no way of telling that a name deleted in one state is still on the roll in another, and calls for it to be scrapped, for the rolls of 4 June 2024 to be restored and for continuous registration that a voter can carry from place to place.
quote: The National Sample Survey Office’s Multiple Indicator Survey (MIS) of 2020-21 found that about 26.8% of the people in rural areas and about 34.6% in urban areas had their current place of residence different from their usual one.
Across all 18 sets of rolls, the deletion rate correlates with the MIS measure of urban work migration at 0.50, a moderate fit, and with Census-based net migration at 0.56.

title: 27.59% Voters Deleted From Ten Karnataka Assembly Constituencies Represented by Muslim MLAs
shows: The Wire carries Vartha Bharati's analysis of figures from Sankalp, a political research consultancy, drawn from the booth-wise lists of names left off Karnataka's draft that the Chief Electoral Officer published. It calls a booth Congress strong where the Congress won 60 per cent or more of the votes in the 2024 Lok Sabha election. Of the 1,07,76,645 names left off that the analysis could place, it finds 22,35,155, or 20.74 per cent, in such booths. In 39 of the 224 seats more than 35 per cent of the names left off are in such booths, and those 39 seats hold 19,85,732 names left off, or 18.4 per cent of the total. The Congress won 26 of the 39 in 2023, the BJP 11 and the Janata Dal (Secular) 2. By Sankalp's estimate Muslims are on average 22 per cent of the roll in the 39 seats, against 12.9 per cent across the state. The roll does not record religion, so a share by religion is an estimate. The article also sets the 10,08,038 additions the Commission recorded against the 7,85,716 applications for inclusion that Sankalp tracked in the Form 9 lists from 16 June 2026, a difference of 2,22,322, and says the Commission has published no reconciliation of the two. It repeats the figures for the ten seats held by Muslim MLAs and for Muslim electors left off as absent and as already enrolled, which the Karnataka Rajya Muslim Okkoota released on 9 November.
quote: According to the data, 22,35,155 deleted names belonged to booths categorised as Congress strong booths, accounting for 20.74% of the total 1,07,76,645 deletions covered in the booth-wise analysis across Karnataka.
These 39 constituencies together account for 19,85,732 deleted names, representing 18.4% of all deletions covered in the booth-wise analysis.

Published 11 November 2026 at 11:12 am IST (post_date 2026-11-11 11:12:16, post_date_gmt 05:42:16), byline Ismail Zaorez. The article says it was first published by Vartha Bharati, whose page was not opened. It calls the names deleted, and they are names left off the draft in the site's words. The 1,07,96,339 it gives as the Commission's total is the site's count of names left off Karnataka's draft, and 22,35,155 and 19,85,732 are 20.74 and 18.43 per cent of the 1,07,76,645 it analysed. It says the analysis covers 99.67 per cent of the names and that 19,846 could not be placed. By the figures it prints, 1,07,76,645 is 99.82 per cent of 1,07,96,339 and 19,694 short of it, and the article does not explain the difference. The 10,08,038 additions and the 1,88,324 deleted through claims and objections agree with the 10.08 lakh added and 1.88 lakh deleted after the draft on the site's Karnataka page. The 39 seats and their split of 26, 11 and 2 are already in Frontline's report of Sankalp's figures (round 39), which gives the share of names left off in those booths within the 39 seats as 42 per cent. The counts of names in Congress strong booths across the state and in the 39 seats, the Muslim share of the 39 seats and the comparison with the Form 9 lists are what this article adds. The figures for the ten seats held by Muslim MLAs, by reason and for the 64 seats where Muslims are 15 per cent or more of the roll are in protest-64, and the figures for the seats of named leaders are not carried. The paragraphs on Uttar Pradesh repeat The Reporters' Collective's investigation of 6 October and the reply of Uttar Pradesh's Chief Electoral Officer, and are not carried. Its questions about the verification process are its own.
